plainLanguage.summary: RFC 1217 is an April 1st joke memo responding to RFC 1216. It pretends to propose extremely slow and inefficient networks, using absurd examples such as reading messages from tank labels and sending signals through the Earth.

sections.title: A Joke Reply to RFC 1216
sections.content:
This is an April 1st joke document, dated 1 April 1991, written as a response to RFC 1216. It presents itself as a proposal from the fictional Consortium for Slow Commotion Research (CSCR) for research on low-speed, low-efficiency networks over “several eons.”

The memo keeps a serious research-proposal tone while describing plainly impractical ideas. Its stated theme is extreme redundancy and slow communication.
sections.plainLanguage: This is an April 1st joke answering RFC 1216. It uses a formal research tone to describe deliberately slow and impractical communication systems.

sections.title: The Proposed Communication Systems
sections.content:
The land system uses M1A1 tanks marked with a 0 or 1 in large yellow paint. An observer reads the tank sequence and radios it to a computer, which decodes the message and sends it back. The undersea proposal uses the guns of the Battleship Missouri to send a signal through the Pacific, with a tank gun as an alternative source. These are presented as serious designs in the memo's joke proposal.

A further undersea design uses neutrino bursts from Batavia National Laboratory through the Earth to a site near Tierra del Fuego, Chile. The memo says the bursts could be sent at a maximum rate of about once every 20 seconds and notes that submarines would need to be scheduled near the receiving site.
sections.plainLanguage: The memo imagines messages read from marked tanks, fired across the ocean, or sent through the Earth as neutrinos. Each proposal makes communication slow or difficult on purpose.

sections.title: Ways to Make the Network Less Efficient
sections.content:
The memo lists further ways to reduce effective throughput. “Anti-Huffman coding” gives the most frequent symbol the longest code, and “minimum likelihood decoding” chooses the least likely interpretation. “Firefly cryptography” uses unrelated jars of fireflies to encode and decode signals, making successful decoding unlikely.

Other proposals include recursively encapsulating each of the 7 OSI layers to create a 49-layer model, using the “Slow Network Management Protocol” with variables in Serbo-Croatian, and routing schemes that delay, alter, or mislabel packets. The memo ends by looking forward to a “protracted and fruitless discussion.” It says security issues are not discussed.
sections.plainLanguage: The memo suggests coding, decoding, management, and routing methods that make messages less likely to arrive quickly or correctly. The joke is that every proposal intentionally makes the network worse.

references.text: RFC 1216, "Gigabit Network Economics and Paradigm Shifts", the memo this RFC answers.
